The paper investigates smooth projective surfaces of general type with geometric genus \(p_g=1\) and irregularity \(q=1\) that are isogenous to a product. Such a surface admits a presentation
\[
S=(C\times F)/G,
\]
where \(C\) and \(F\) are smooth projective curves of genus at least two and \(G\) is a finite group acting freely on \(C\times F\). The action may preserve the two factors or, when the curves are isomorphic, interchange them. Because the quotient is free, \(S\) is smooth and its numerical invariants can be computed directly from the genera of the curves and the order of \(G\). In particular, the condition \(p_g=q=1\) implies \(\chi(\mathcal O_S)=1\), and hence \(K_S^2=8\).

The main objective is to determine all possible groups, curve genera, quotient maps, and group actions that can occur under these constraints. The irregularity condition strongly restricts the genera of the quotient curves \(C/G\) and \(F/G\), while the equality \(\chi(\mathcal O_S)=1\) imposes the numerical relation
\[
(g(C)-1)(g(F)-1)=|G|.
\]
The classification problem can therefore be translated into the study of finite group actions on curves with prescribed branching data.

Using the theory of branched Galois coverings, the authors encode these actions through generating systems for finite groups. The Riemann–Hurwitz formula limits the possible signatures of the coverings, and the requirement that the diagonal action on \(C\times F\) be free imposes additional compatibility conditions: nontrivial elements that have fixed points on one factor cannot have fixed points on the other. These numerical and group-theoretic restrictions reduce the problem to a finite collection of cases, which are then analyzed individually.

The resulting classification identifies every surface of this type, up to the relevant equivalence of group actions. For each admissible case, it determines the finite group \(G\), the genera of \(C\) and \(F\), the branching signatures of the quotient maps, and the corresponding families in the moduli space of surfaces of general type. It also distinguishes the possible types of actions and explains when different presentations yield isomorphic or deformation-equivalent surfaces.

Thus, the paper gives a complete description of projective surfaces with \(p_g=q=1\) that are isogenous to a product. Beyond producing a list of possibilities, it clarifies how the geometry of these surfaces is governed by the interaction between branched coverings of curves, finite-group actions, and the freeness condition on the product. The work therefore provides a precise structural picture of this important class of irregular surfaces of general type.

# A Projective Surface

A projective surface is a two-dimensional geometric object studied in projective geometry and algebraic geometry. Unlike an ordinary surface in three-dimensional Euclidean space, it is defined within projective space, where points at infinity are included. This framework allows parallel lines to intersect and often gives geometric constructions a more unified and elegant form.

In algebraic geometry, a projective surface is commonly described as the set of solutions to one or more homogeneous polynomial equations in projective space. For example, a surface in the projective space \(\mathbb{P}^3\) may be defined by an equation

\[
F(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)=0,
\]

where \(F\) is a homogeneous polynomial. Homogeneity ensures that the equation is unchanged when all coordinates are multiplied by the same nonzero scalar, as required for projective coordinates.

The degree of the defining polynomial plays an important role in the geometry of the surface. A polynomial of degree one defines a projective plane, while one of degree two defines a quadric surface. Cubic and quartic surfaces have more complicated structures and are central objects of research. Their properties may include singular points, families of curves, symmetries, and distinctive topological features.

Projective surfaces are useful because projective space is compact in the appropriate geometric sense. Intersections that might disappear “at infinity” in affine geometry remain visible in the projective setting. This makes it possible to formulate powerful results, such as Bézout’s theorem, which relates the degrees of algebraic varieties to the number of their intersection points.

The study of projective surfaces connects algebra, geometry, topology, and complex analysis. By examining their equations, singularities, curves, and transformations, mathematicians gain insight into both the local and global behavior of geometric spaces.

counterfactuals.output:
A **projective surface isogenous to a product** is a smooth projective surface \(S\) admitting a finite étale cover by a product of smooth curves of genus at least \(2\). Equivalently,
\[
S \cong (C_1\times C_2)/G,
\]
where \(g(C_i)\ge 2\) and a finite group \(G\) acts freely on \(C_1\times C_2\). The surface is of **unmixed type** if \(G\) preserves each factor and of **mixed type** if some elements interchange the factors.

The paper classifies such surfaces with
\[
p_g(S)=q(S)=0
\quad\text{(equivalently, } \chi(\mathcal O_S)=1\text{),}
\]
determining the possible groups and group actions—and hence the corresponding deformation/moduli families—in both the unmixed and mixed cases.
